passages.title: The Lighthouse Keeper
passages.text: The lighthouse stood white against the grey sea. Mara had kept its lamp for eleven years, and she knew every gull by its cry. That night the storm took the radio, the spare bulb, and — worst of all — her certainty. When the small boat appeared between waves, she had only the old oil lamp and her own judgement.

questions.explain: It guides the boat despite the storm.
Radio, bulb and certainty are gone.

passages.title: Opinion: Phones in Schools
passages.text: Banning phones sounds decisive, but it confuses the tool with the behaviour. Phones can distract, yet they can also document experiments, translate words, and time sprints. The fair rule is not a ban but managed use: pouches in class, freedom at lunch, consequences for misuse.

questions.explain: Pouches in class, freedom at lunch.

passages.title: Volcanoes Explained
passages.text: Volcanoes form where plates pull apart or collide. Magma rises because it is less dense than rock. Thin, runny lava flows far; thick lava traps gas and explodes. Ash can cool the planet for a year, even as lava rebuilds the land.

passages.text: The bus breathes fog. / Windows bloom with frost-flowers. / A girl counts stops like beads. / The city slides past, grey as a sleeve.

passages.title: Should School Start Later?
passages.text:
Nobody learns well at 8am — at least, that is what the sleep researchers keep telling us. Teenagers' body clocks shift later during adolescence, which means a 9am start asks students to think hardest exactly when their brains are still booting up. Several Australian schools that trialled later starts reported calmer first periods and fewer late arrivals.

Critics argue the day would simply finish later, pushing sport and part-time jobs into the evening. That is a fair concern, but it confuses scheduling with learning. If the goal of school is learning, the timetable should follow the evidence about when learning happens best, not when buses have always run.

A later start will not fix everything — phones at midnight undo any timetable. Yet of all the reforms debated in education, moving first period later is among the cheapest and most studied. We should try what the evidence supports.

passages.title: How Vaccines Train the Immune System
passages.text:
A vaccine is a training session for your immune system. Most vaccines contain a harmless preview of a germ — a weakened virus, an inactivated one, or just a fragment of its outer coat. Your body studies this preview and builds memory cells: specialised defenders that remember the invader's shape for years.

If the real germ arrives later, those memory cells recognise it immediately and multiply into an army within days instead of weeks. That speed is the whole trick. Many illnesses only become dangerous because they outrun a first-time immune response; with memory cells waiting, the race is over before symptoms begin.

This is also why most vaccines cannot give you the disease they prevent. A fragment of a coat cannot build a house, and an inactivated virus cannot replicate. The training happens without the battle.

options: Respond within days instead of weeks

passages.title: The Night the River Rose
passages.text:
Lena woke to the sound of the rain arguing with the roof. By dawn the creek behind the house had become something else entirely — brown, hurried, carrying branches like messages it couldn't deliver. Her father stood on the veranda with his hands in his pockets, watching the water take the fence posts one by one.

'We go now,' he said, not loudly. Lena carried the photo albums; her brother carried the dog, who objected to everything. They waded to the neighbour's ute with their trousers rolled, laughing in the nervous way people laugh when they have decided not to be afraid.

By afternoon the street was a slow canal. From the evacuation centre on the hill, Lena watched a wheelie bin sail past like a small green boat, and understood for the first time what her grandmother meant when she said the river remembers where it used to go.
